summary: I classified all 375 committed events in every journal.jsonl across artifacts/simulations_v4, artifacts/simulations_v3 and artifacts/matched_pairs by hand-checked pattern, read all 543 event-quality reviews, and read the world and review prompts and the commit path in trajectory.py. 162 of 375 committed events (43%) are an item in transit, a device alerting, or an explicit restatement that nothing changed; in the only three runs long enough to read as a story it is 55%, 64% and 54%. 92 of those (24.5% of the whole record) are the exact category that BOTH the world prompt (world_mind.py:126-130) and the event-quality review (world_mind.py:331-332) name as forbidden, and every one of them passed review. The review is inverted: it passes bookkeeping proposals at 71% and everything else at 63%, and 39 of its 173 non-PASS verdicts reject an event whose subject is a named person on the grounds that it is 'a device acting on its own' - which is how six of eight matched-pair B runs end NO_AT_CUTOFF on evidence that says the person returns every document within a day. The granularity concern the implementer raised is real, is quantified below, and is worse than they framed it: it does not merely make the traces ugly, it changes the terminal answers.

findings.title: Interface bookkeeping is the plurality of the committed record; in the long runs it is the majority
findings.evidence: All 31 journals under artifacts/{simulations_v4,simulations_v3,matched_pairs}: 162/375 committed events (43.2%) are an item arriving/being transmitted/queued, a device alerting (phone buzzes, notification appears, lock screen shows, phone rings), or an explicit no-change restatement. Per run: simulations_v3/case3_group 60/94 (64%), simulations_v3/unseen4_holiday_deposit 44/81 (54%), simulations_v3/case2_negotiation 22/40 (55%), simulations_v3/unseen2_feedback 8/19 (42%), matched_pairs/a2_unresponsive__r3 7/9 (78%). Worked example: case2_negotiation commits the SAME message arriving unread six times - e548, e554 (16:47), e575, e579, e586 (16:48), e591 (16:49). case3_group commits 12 separate events that are only Kwame's phone buzzing while he never acts (e187, e241, e418, e633, e850, e959, e1172, e1272, e1473, e1556 and more). unseen2_feedback commits one email arriving three times at the same instant (e250, e256, e270 all at 2026-07-28T18:10:10) plus e275 'sits unread in Ravi's inbox'.
findings.why_it_matters: The area's central question - is this a world about people or about software - answers 'about software' for every run long enough to matter. A reader of artifacts/simulations_v3/case3_group/trajectory.md does not encounter four housemates arranging a dinner; they encounter a notification log. Worse, this bookkeeping consumes the step budget: case3_group and unseen4_holiday_deposit both hit the 250-step ceiling and returned status 'incomplete' (runtime_metrics.json), never reaching their cutoff, having spent 60 and 44 of their committed steps on phones.
findings.suggested_fix: Make availability a code-owned property of a journal item (it is already tracked as `for`/`observed`) and stop admitting delivery, transit and alert hops as committed events at all, so a committed event is only ever a person doing or perceiving something.

findings.title: The event-quality review is inverted: it admits the non-events its own prompt forbids and rejects real human acts as machinery
findings.evidence: Across 543 reviews (PASS 355 / REVISE 169 / ACTOR_TURN_REQUIRED 19), the PASS rate on delivery/alert/no-change proposals is 71% (161/227) versus 63% (194/308) on everything else. 92 committed events are literally 'a restatement that nothing has changed -- still unread, still waiting, still busy', which world_mind.py:331-332 lists under REVISE and world_mind.py:126-130 tells the world never to emit: e.g. case3_group e1397 'Tomas's phone remains on the table with the lock screen still showing the unread group chat notifications', case3_group e1473 'Kwame's phone continues to accumulate unread group chat notifications', case2_negotiation e591, unseen4 e211 and e1103 - all PASSED. In the other direction, 39 of 173 non-PASS reviews reject a proposal whose grammatical subject is a named person, citing a device: 'Aisha prints the lease document' REVISED six times across b1_okafor_herrera, __r2, __r3 and __r4 ('the printer printing is a device acting on its own'); 'Margaret scans the signed lease using her printer/scanner and saves the PDF to her computer' REVISED (b2_thornbury_lim); 'Marcus checks the hall booking system and sees that the hall is held for the 14th' REVISED as 'machinery operation' (a1_responsive__r3) - all of which world_mind.py:301-313 explicitly instructs it to PASS.
findings.why_it_matters: The only content control in the system pushes exactly the wrong way, and it decides answers. matched_pairs/b1_okafor_herrera__r3 committed ONE event (the seed) because all four world proposals were refused as printers and scanners; the terminal is NO_AT_CUTOFF for a woman whose evidence says she returns documents within a day. Six of the eight B-pair runs (b1 __r2/__r3/__r4, b2 base/__r2/__r3) return NO_AT_CUTOFF, and in each the actor's own recorded decision was to sign and send.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the device/machinery limb of EVENT_REVIEW_SYSTEM entirely and keep only the two checks the traces show it gets right - 'already in the record' and 'restatement that nothing has changed' - applied to the bookkeeping family it currently waves through.

findings.title: Event granularity is uncontrolled and it produces wrong terminal answers, not just ugly traces
findings.evidence: matched_pairs/b2_thornbury_lim spends all 8 of its committed events inside 2 minutes (08:00:00-08:02:00) on e23 'notices the email', e31 'opens and sees the attachment', e37 'opens, downloads the PDF, and prints it', e40 'sees the attachment and reads the first page', e53 'signs the printed lease document with a pen', e60 'signs the lease with a pen' (again), e63 'places the signed lease on her desk next to the printer/scanner'. trajectory.md then records margaret_thornbury deciding to sign-and-email FOUR separate times, with the world answering '(no concrete event yet)' to the last three; the world's own final judgment reads 'Margaret has the signed lease on her desk and the printer/scanner is nearby. She will scan it to create a PDF' and commits nothing. Terminal: NO_AT_CUTOFF. Symmetrically, 60-64% of world judgments in the long runs produce no event at all (case3_group 164/268, unseen4 147/231, case2 65/108).
findings.why_it_matters: The judge is correct that no send exists, so the NO is honest about the record - but the record is wrong about the person. The evidence said she returns every document within a day and she decided to; the runtime spent the run on the preamble and then reported that she did not. This is the failure mode the runtime is supposed to prevent, arriving through granularity instead of through actor behaviour.
findings.suggested_fix: Require the world to emit the completed unit of what a person was doing (the thing the fragments add up to), and treat a proposal that is a stage of an attempt already in flight - opening, printing, placing on a desk - as no event rather than as progress.

findings.title: MAX_EVENTS_PER_INSTANT polices seconds while the granularity problem lives in minutes and hours
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:56 MAX_EVENTS_PER_INSTANT = 3; trajectory.py:262-267 counts events whose `t` equals the exact current instant; trajectory.py:369-374 only applies MIN_STEP_ON_A_CROWDED_INSTANT when `delta.total_seconds()` is zero. So any non-'now' duration lands on a fresh, empty instant and the guard never fires. matched_pairs/c1_against_stereotype puts 15 events in the minute 2026-09-09T08:00, then 6 in 08:01, 7 in 08:02, 4 in 08:03 - 32 of its 33 events inside one hour - without tripping the guard once. simulations_v3/case3_group puts 19 events in the hour 2026-10-08T09. The guard is also leaky at its own resolution: 4 events share one exact second three times (case3_group 2026-10-06T18:03:10; unseen4 2026-09-13T19:40:00 and 2026-09-14T22:17:00) because two chains scheduled from different origins can land on the same second after the count was taken.
findings.why_it_matters: The implementer's own diagnosis is confirmed exactly: the only structural brake on subdividing time operates two to three orders of magnitude below where the subdivision happens, so it provides false assurance that time density is controlled.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a per-actor events-per-hour ceiling alongside the per-instant one, and floor `after` whenever the current hour is already crowded, not only when the world says 'now'.

findings.title: Duplicate detection is exact-string only, so near-identical and directly contradictory events both commit
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:275-279 builds `already` from `contained(description).casefold()` and world_mind.py:246-253 tests membership exactly. 55 of 375 committed events (14.7%) are a >=0.85 normalised match of an earlier event in the same run. Concrete: simulations_v3/unseen4_holiday_deposit e250 'Dev's private message arrives on Ruth's phone but she does not notice it' and e256 'Dev's private message arrives on Ruth's phone and she notices it' - BOTH committed at 2026-09-13T21:11:00, a flat contradiction at one instant. case3_group e67 'The message from Ines arrives on Tomas's phone, appearing in the group chat notification' and e641 '...appearing as a group chat notification' - normalised ratio 1.00, byte-different, both committed. unseen2_feedback e250/e256/e270 (three arrivals of one email at one instant). matched_pairs/b2_thornbury_lim e53 and e60 (Margaret signs the lease with a pen, twice, at 08:01:00). matched_pairs/a1_responsive__r3 e31 and e41 (Marcus notices Dana's message, twice, at 08:05:00).
findings.why_it_matters: The world prompt's rule 'the same thing cannot occur twice' is enforced only against a literal rewrite, which the model almost never produces. The unseen4 pair means the ledger simultaneously records that Ruth did and did not notice the same message at the same second - a fact no downstream reader can reconcile.
findings.suggested_fix: Compare against committed and pending descriptions with a normalised similarity threshold rather than exact casefold equality, and reject a proposal that asserts the negation of an already-committed observation for the same (actor, item).

findings.title: evaluation/interface_mechanics.py under-reports machinery by about sixfold; its 7% figure is a count of one preposition
findings.evidence: `python3 evaluation/interface_mechanics.py` over all runs reports 26/358 = 7%. 24 of its 28 hits on my snapshot are the literal phrase 'arrives in <inbox|group chat>'. The regex at evaluation/interface_mechanics.py:23-38 misses every one of these committed events: 'The message arrives on Marcus Bell's phone' (simulations_v4/a1_r1 e21 - 'arrives on' is not 'arrives in'), 'Dana's message arrives at Marcus's phone and is queued for delivery' (a2_unresponsive__r4 e22), 'Kwame's phone buzzes with the group chat notifications' (case3_group e241), 'The notification from Ines's message appears on Tomas's phone's lock screen' (case3_group e668 - the regex requires 'notification appears' adjacent), 'Bea's phone displays the new notification...' (case3_group e1593), 'Tomas's phone remains on the table with the lock screen still showing...' (case3_group e1397), 'The messages from Priya remain unread on Dmitri's phone' (case2 e591), 'The message is transmitted to Marcus's phone, which is off' (a2_unresponsive__r2 e20), 'Marian Prowse's phone rings' (unseen4 e1246), 'The terminal displays a pairing code on its screen' (c1 e163), 'The support system displays a message...' (c1 e268). It also has false positives: case2_negotiation e491 is Priya sending a follow-up message, flagged only for its trailing 'arrives in the seller's inbox' clause.
findings.why_it_matters: The module docstring says it exists 'so that a claim about how human a trajectory looks can be checked instead of asserted'. As written it licenses the assertion it was built to test: it will report single-digit machinery on a record that is 43% machinery, and it is the number a reader is most likely to trust.
findings.suggested_fix: Classify by grammatical subject - is the actor of the sentence a person or an item/device - rather than by a phrase list, and report the no-change restatements ('remains unread', 'still showing', 'does not notice') as a separate counted category.

findings.title: artifacts/simulations_v4 was being written while this review ran and is too thin to support any claim
findings.evidence: artifacts/simulations_v4/ grew from 5 to 8 run directories during this session; at snapshot time a1_r1 had 4 committed events, a2_r1 1, b1_r1 3, b2_r1 1, b2_r2 4, case1_cold_email 4, unseen1 2. Three directories (b1_r1, case3_group, unseen1) had 0 of 21 artifact files at first listing.
findings.why_it_matters: v4 is described as the newest evidence but no v4 run yet contains enough committed events to distinguish an improved event-meaning policy from a run that simply stopped early; the v4 machinery share looks better only because the runs are shorter. Any before/after claim from v4 is currently unsupported.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-run the v4 set to completion and re-measure machinery share only on runs that reached their cutoff or resolved.
